lesson.title: From Balanced Equation to Beaker: Molar Ratios in Solution
lesson.summary: Combining molarity with the mole-to-mole ratios from a balanced equation lets you calculate exactly how much of one dissolved substance is needed to react completely with a measured volume of another, all without ever using a balance.
lesson.body:
Molarity turns volume into a stand-in for moles. Because molarity is defined as moles of solute per liter of solution, the relationship moles equals molarity times volume means that if you know the concentration and volume of a solution, you already know how many moles of solute it contains, no weighing required. A balanced chemical equation, meanwhile, gives you fixed, whole-number mole-to-mole ratios between every reactant and product. Put those two ideas together and you get a powerful shortcut: starting from the volume and concentration of one solution, you can calculate the volume of a second solution needed to react with it exactly, completely bypassing the balance entirely.

This matters constantly in real lab work. Chemists routinely need to know how much of one reagent solution to add to fully consume another, whether they are running a precipitation reaction, preparing a specific product, or setting up the titrations and back titrations covered later in this unit. The logic is always the same four-step chain: convert the known solution's volume and molarity into moles, use the balanced equation's coefficients as a mole ratio to convert to moles of the substance you want, then convert those moles back into a volume (or mass) using that substance's own molarity (or molar mass).

Here is a worked example. Silver nitrate reacts with calcium chloride in solution according to the balanced equation 2 AgNO3(aq) + CaCl2(aq) to 2 AgCl(s) + Ca(NO3)2(aq). Suppose you have 25.0 mL of 0.100 M CaCl2 and want to know exactly what volume of 0.250 M AgNO3 is needed to react with it completely, with nothing left over on either side.

First, find the moles of CaCl2 available: 0.0250 L times 0.100 mol/L equals 0.00250 mol CaCl2. Next, use the mole ratio from the balanced equation. The coefficients show 2 mol AgNO3 react with every 1 mol CaCl2, so moles of AgNO3 needed equals 2 times 0.00250 mol, which is 0.00500 mol AgNO3. Finally, convert that amount back into a volume using the AgNO3 solution's own molarity: volume equals moles divided by molarity, so 0.00500 mol divided by 0.250 mol/L equals 0.0200 L, or 20.0 mL.

So 20.0 mL of 0.250 M AgNO3 will react exactly with the 25.0 mL of 0.100 M CaCl2, precipitating out all the chloride as solid AgCl. This same moles-of-known, mole-ratio, moles-of-unknown, volume-of-unknown pattern is the backbone of essentially every solution stoichiometry problem you will meet from here on, including titration and back titration calculations later in this unit.
